strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important issue: whether the widely used Biasing Features metric truly measures CoT faithfulness or instead conflates unfaithfulness with incompleteness. The distinction is conceptually well motivated and clearly explained.

The empirical evaluation is broad and systematic, covering three multi-hop reasoning datasets, three instruction-tuned models, three hint types, and multiple complementary faithfulness metrics (Filler Tokens, FUR, faithful@k, Logit Lens, and Causal Mediation Analysis).

The new faithful@k adaptation provides a useful way to test whether apparent unfaithfulness is partly explained by limited inference-time sampling budget, and the observed increases under the Professor hint offer concrete evidence for the incompleteness hypothesis.

The Causal Mediation Analysis is a valuable addition: it moves beyond hint-verbalization checks by estimating direct and indirect effects, showing that non-verbalized hints can still have measurable causal influence through the generated CoT.

The paper is generally well organized, with clear explanations of metrics, methods, and results. Reproducibility details are relatively strong: code is promised, prompts and hyperparameters are documented, compute details are provided, and the LLM-as-judge is validated against human annotations.
The discussion and limitations section appropriately acknowledges constraints and recommends a broader interpretability toolkit rather than relying solely on hint-based evaluations.
weaknesses: The central argument relies heavily on alternative faithfulness metrics such as Filler Tokens and FUR. These metrics are themselves imperfect proxies with their own assumptions, so evidence that they disagree with Biasing Features does not conclusively establish that CoTs are faithful rather than merely differently measured.

The faithful@k interpretation is not fully airtight: increasing k can also raise the chance of observing a faithful sample simply due to stochastic generation, even if the model is genuinely unfaithful in most samples. The paper does not provide a formal model to distinguish stochastic verbalization from completeness.

The Causal Mediation Analysis depends on strong identification assumptions (e.g., no unmeasured confounding, consistency, and correct model specification). These assumptions are not tested or discussed in depth, and the estimated NDE/NIE may not have a clean causal interpretation in this setting.

The LLM-as-judge used for hint verbalization has low precision (36%) and recall (31%) against human annotations. Although the authors provide a robustness check, false negatives could still affect the conclusions about which CoTs are considered unfaithful.

The experiments are limited to relatively small models (3B-8B parameters) and multiple-choice reasoning tasks. The paper acknowledges this, but the broader claim that CoTs can be faithful without hint verbalization may not generalize to larger or specialized reasoning models, or to open-ended generation settings.

The Logit Lens evidence is correlational and restricted to MHA outputs; hint-related tokens appearing in top-5 predictions do not by themselves prove that the hint is being used in a causally relevant reasoning process.

The paper critiques Biasing Features effectively but does not offer a complete replacement definition of faithfulness. faithful@k measures the probability of verbalizing a hint under sampling, which is not identical to faithfulness in the broader sense.

Some framing in the title and abstract may be broader than the evidence: the paper convincingly shows that Biasing Features can mislabel some CoTs, but it does not fully settle whether CoT is or is not explainability in the broader sense debated in prior work.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely question: whether the widely-used Biasing Features (hint-verbalization) metric actually licenses the strong 'CoT is not explainability' conclusions drawn in recent work. The paper's reframing of apparent 'unfaithfulness' as 'incompleteness' is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution to the interpretability literature.

Methodological triangulation is a real strength. The paper does not rest on a single counter-metric; it combines (i) cross-metric comparison with Filler Tokens and FUR, (ii) a faithful@k sampling-based analysis, (iii) Logit Lens layer-wise probing, and (iv) Causal Mediation Analysis (NDE/NIE). This multi-method approach makes the central empirical claim (that Biasing Features overstates unfaithfulness) more convincing than any single experiment would.

The experiments are reasonably systematic across three datasets (StrategyQA, OpenbookQA, ARC-Easy), three models, and three hint types (Professor, Metadata, Black Squares), with 95% bootstrap CIs and extensive appendix tables (Tables 1–5, Figures 9–19). The three-hint-type design is well-motivated and the differential behavior across hint types (e.g., Professor vs. Black Squares in faithful@k) is informative.

Reproducibility is strong: code is promised upon publication, the LLM-as-judge prompt (DSPy signature) is given verbatim (Fig. 20), and the FUR hyperparameter selection procedure is documented (Appendix A). The manual annotation of 100 instances with an explicit confusion matrix (Fig. 17) and the robustness re-run on the strictly-unfaithful subset (Figs. 18–19) are exactly the right kind of validation.

The paper is clearly written and the narrative is well structured, with explicit takeaway boxes (T1–T3.2) that map claims to evidence. The limitations section is candid about compute and model-scale constraints.
weaknesses: The central conceptual claim rests on a particular definition of faithfulness (simulatability/alignment with the true reasoning process), which is asserted rather than argued against competing definitions. The paper's conclusion that CoT 'can be faithful without hint verbalization' is only as strong as this definitional choice; a reader who accepts verbalization-as-faithfulness will not be moved by the empirical results.

The Causal Mediation Analysis is the weakest link. Since the CoT is generated conditioned on the hinted input, a non-zero NIE is essentially guaranteed by construction for any model whose CoT carries any information about the input; it does not by itself distinguish genuine reasoning from post-hoc rationalization. The paper acknowledges this in passing but still draws the fairly strong conclusion (T3.1) that CoTs 'mediate part of the hint's effect rather than being purely post-hoc.' The NDE/NIE magnitudes are tiny in absolute terms (1e-6 to 1e-4) and the comparison across models/tasks is noisy, making the interpretive claims fragile.

faithful@k is an adaptation of pass@k that measures whether *at least one* of k samples verbalizes the hint. This is a capability/coverage measure, not a faithfulness rate, and the paper sometimes slides between the two (e.g., 'faithful@k ... captures output variability beyond greedy decoding'). A model that verbalizes the hint in 1/16 samples gets faithful@k≈1 while remaining unfaithful on the vast majority of draws; the inference that unfaithfulness 'is consistent with incompleteness' therefore overstates what the metric shows. The link between faithful@k and 'tight token limits' is also indirect (the metric varies sampling, not the token budget).

Generalization is limited: only 3–8B instruction-tuned models are tested, and the paper explicitly excludes specialized reasoning models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1-style), which are precisely the models at the center of the 'CoT is not explainability' debate. Several conclusions (e.g., that LLaMA-3-8B produces degenerate CoTs) may be model-specific artifacts rather than general phenomena.

The LLM-as-judge has low precision (36%) and recall (31%) despite 80% accuracy. The paper argues false positives are less concerning because it focuses on negatives, but the low recall means some CoTs counted as 'non-verbalizing' may in fact verbalize, biasing the very quantities the paper is built on. The mitigation (re-running on the strictly-unfaithful subset) is helpful but does not fully resolve this for the main analyses.

The Black Squares and Metadata results cut against the paper's own narrative: faithful@k stays flat for these hints, which the authors interpret as these hints inducing genuine post-hoc rationalization, but this inconsistency is under-discussed and suggests the 'incompleteness' explanation may be hint-type-specific rather than general.

Some of the critique of Biasing Features (that it measures verbalized sensitivity rather than faithfulness) is already implicit in prior work (e.g., Lanham et al.; Zaman and Srivastava 2025, cited), so the novelty is more in the systematic multi-metric rebuttal than in the core observation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question: whether the widely used Biasing Features metric conflates unfaithfulness with incompleteness, and whether conclusions that CoT is 'not explainability' are overstated.

The empirical effort is broad and systematic: three instruction-tuned models (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, gemma-3-4b-it), three multi-hop datasets, three hint types, and several complementary analyses (Biasing Features, Filler Tokens, FUR, faithful@k, Causal Mediation Analysis, and Logit Lens).

The paper provides useful negative results: Biasing Features labels most answer-changing CoTs as unfaithful (up to 80–100% in some settings), while alternative metrics such as Filler Tokens and FUR classify a non-trivial fraction (often 20–50%) as faithful, indicating that different metrics capture different notions of faithfulness.

The faithful@k analysis is a reasonable adaptation of pass@k to quantify how often multiple sampled CoTs contain a verbalized hint, and it yields the interesting observation that faithful@k can rise sharply with k for the Professor hint, suggesting that some apparent unfaithfulness is sampling-related.

The causal mediation analysis, though imperfect, attempts to move beyond correlational evaluation and provides evidence that non-verbalized hinted CoTs can have non-zero natural indirect effects, challenging a purely post-hoc rationalization account.

The paper is generally well-organized, with clear figures and a detailed appendix covering prompts, hyperparameters, control metrics, compute details, and LLM-as-judge prompts, which supports reproducibility if the promised code is released.

The discussion and conclusion appropriately caution against relying solely on hint-verbalization-based metrics and recommend a broader interpretability toolkit, which is a valuable methodological message for the CoT faithfulness literature.
weaknesses: The core conceptual distinction between 'unfaithfulness' and 'incompleteness' is under-theorized and not rigorously operationalized. Under common definitions (e.g., Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020), an explanation that omits a causally active hint is arguably unfaithful, not merely incomplete. The paper shows that CoTs can be causally relevant without verbalizing the hint, but it does not show that they faithfully represent the hint's influence.

The alternative metrics used to argue that Biasing Features is misleading measure fundamentally different constructs. Filler Tokens tests whether the CoT is causally necessary for the prediction, and FUR tests whether unlearning individual reasoning steps changes the prediction; neither tests whether the CoT verbalizes or faithfully represents the prompt hint. Thus 'faithful under other metrics' does not directly refute Biasing Features' finding about hint verbalization.

The faithful@k analysis is not a manipulation of inference-time token budget. It samples multiple independent outputs and conditions on answer-changing samples, so the abstract's claim that 'larger inference-time token budgets greatly increase hint verbalization' is unsupported. The pass@k adaptation is also non-standard because n is defined as the number of answer-changing samples rather than all generated samples, which complicates interpretation.

The Causal Mediation Analysis equations (6)–(7) do not correspond to the standard NDE/NIE decomposition. In particular, the NIE is computed with the input fixed at x rather than x_h (or vice versa depending on decomposition), so NDE and NIE do not sum to the total effect. No total effect or proportion-mediated estimate is reported, and mediator-outcome confounding is not addressed, weakening the causal claims.

The LLM-as-judge used to determine hint verbalization has low precision (36%) and recall (31%) in the human-annotated sample (Appendix D). Since all Biasing Features labels and many downstream comparisons depend on this judge, measurement error may substantially affect the reported rates. The stricter lexical-subset robustness check helps but does not fully resolve this concern.

The FUR control metrics show variable and sometimes low unlearning efficiency (e.g., 12.7–38.8 for gemma-3-4b-it in Table 2) and specificity trade-offs. If reasoning steps are not reliably removed, FUR-based faithfulness estimates are difficult to interpret as evidence about model reasoning.

The Logit Lens analysis is exploratory and applies unembedding to MHA outputs rather than the residual stream, with no control comparisons. The claims about hint-related token activation across layers are therefore suggestive but not strong mechanistic evidence.

The experimental scope is limited to 3B–8B models and three multi-hop datasets; larger or dedicated reasoning models are absent due to compute constraints. Generalization to state-of-the-art LLMs and real-world reasoning settings is therefore unclear.

The paper's central positive claim—'CoT can be faithful without hint verbalization'—overstates the evidence. A more accurate summary is that CoTs can be causally relevant without verbalizing the hint, which is compatible with their being incomplete or unfaithful as explanations of the hint's influence.

Reproducibility is not yet fully demonstrated because the code is only promised for release upon publication, and the exact hint randomization, sample exclusion criteria, and handling of degenerate CoTs are not fully specified in the main text.

strengths: The paper makes a compelling, well-supported case that the Biasing Features metric conflates unfaithfulness with incompleteness, using a multi-metric, multi-model, multi-dataset evaluation that goes beyond prior single-metric claims.

It introduces faithful@k, a principled adaptation of pass@k to faithfulness, and shows that larger inference-time budgets substantially increase hint verbalization (up to ~90%), providing direct evidence for the incompleteness hypothesis.

It complements text-based metrics with Causal Mediation Analysis and Logit Lens analyses, demonstrating that non-verbalized hints can still causally mediate predictions and leave internal traces, which strengthens the central claim beyond correlational evidence.

The empirical setup is extensive (5 models including 70B/32B reasoning models, 3 multi-hop datasets, 3 hint types) and the paper provides detailed implementation, hyperparameters, compute details, and code availability, supporting reproducibility.

The paper is candid about limitations (LLM-as-judge reliability, cherry-picking concerns, completeness vs. exhaustiveness) and frames its conclusions cautiously, avoiding overclaiming that all CoTs are faithful.
weaknesses: The main unfaithfulness labels depend on an LLM-as-judge with low precision/recall (36%/31%) using gpt-oss-20b; although the authors provide robustness checks, the primary results are not re-run with the more accurate gpt-4o judge, leaving uncertainty about how judge errors affect the headline numbers.

The alternative metrics used to show that many CoTs are 'faithful' (Filler Tokens and FUR) are themselves imperfect proxies; Filler Tokens may be confounded by output format, and FUR relies on unlearning quality and only applies to a subset of instances, so the conclusion that Biasing Features is inconsistent with true faithfulness is suggestive rather than definitive.

The Causal Mediation Analysis reports very small effect sizes (often on the order of 1e-5 to 1e-9) and does not fully discuss identification assumptions or the validity of text-based interventions on the CoT mediator; practical significance of these effects remains unclear.

faithful@k could cherry-pick favorable samples, and the paper's aggregate arguments (monotonic increase under Professor, flatness under other hints) do not fully rule out the alternative interpretation that the model is only occasionally faithful rather than merely incomplete.

Generalization to larger and reasoning models is limited to a subset of tasks and uses 4-bit quantization / a thinking-mode model; Qwen-3-32B even shows negative indirect effects under the Metadata hint, indicating model-specific behavior that complicates broad conclusions.

The conceptual boundary between 'incompleteness' and 'unfaithfulness' is not grounded in a ground-truth measure of the model's actual reasoning process, so the paper's central reinterpretation, while plausible, ultimately depends on proxy metrics and may not settle the debate.

strengths: Timely and important critique of a widely used CoT faithfulness metric, challenging the field's reliance on hint verbalization as a proxy for faithfulness.
Comprehensive empirical study across 3 multi-hop QA datasets, 5 models (including reasoning models), 3 hint types, and multiple faithfulness metrics.
Introduces faithful@k, an adaptation of pass@k that provides a useful diagnostic for distinguishing incompleteness from unfaithfulness, with clear divergence across hint types.
Uses causal mediation analysis (NDE/NIE) to provide evidence that non-verbalized CoTs can causally mediate hint influence, going beyond correlational analyses.
Includes logit lens analysis showing hint-related concepts propagate through internal layers, complementing behavioral results.
Generalizes key findings to larger and reasoning-specialized models (Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen-3-32B), with appropriate caveats.
Transparent about limitations (judge precision/recall, cherry-picking concern, completeness vs. exhaustiveness) and provides robustness checks on stricter subsets and with a stronger judge.
Well-organized, clear figures, and detailed appendices with implementation, prompts, hyperparameters, and qualitative examples; code is available.
weaknesses: The alternative metrics used to claim 'faithfulness' (Filler Tokens, FUR) primarily measure causal dependence or parametric alignment, not whether the CoT accurately reflects the model's true reasoning; equating them with faithfulness may overstate the conclusion.
The LLM-as-judge for verbalization has low precision (36%) and recall (31%); although robustness checks are provided, false negatives could still bias estimates and weaken the central comparison.

The large faithful@k gains occur mainly under the Professor hint; under Black Squares and Metadata, faithful@k remains flat, so the broad claim that much apparent unfaithfulness is due to tight token limits is not uniformly supported across hint types.

Causal mediation estimates may depend on how CoT samples are drawn (single vs. multiple samples), and the paper does not fully clarify the sampling procedure for NDE/NIE; mediation through a non-verbalized CoT does not by itself establish that the CoT is a faithful explanation.
Generalization to larger/reasoning models is incomplete: FUR is not evaluated for those models, and only a subset of tasks/models is used, limiting the strength of the generalization claim.
The paper lacks human evaluation of explanation faithfulness; it relies on automated metrics and an imperfect judge, leaving the ground-truth notion of faithfulness underspecified.

The distinction between 'incompleteness' and 'unfaithfulness' is largely definitional; the paper does not fully resolve whether omitting a causally relevant hint should count as unfaithfulness in interpretability practice.
Experiments are limited to multiple-choice QA; it is unclear how the findings extend to open-ended generation or other reasoning domains.
The code availability footnote appears incomplete in the manuscript, which could hinder reproducibility if not an anonymization artifact.

strengths: The paper targets a real and important methodological issue: the field has increasingly treated hint-verbalization (Biasing Features) as the operational definition of CoT faithfulness, and a careful critique of that conflation is valuable. The framing that a CoT is a lossy natural-language compression of distributed transformer computation, and that non-verbalization therefore need not imply unfaithfulness, is a sensible and well-articulated argument.

The experimental scope is broad and systematic: three datasets (StrategyQA, OpenbookQA, ARC-Easy), three hint types (Professor, Metadata, Black Squares), several instruction-tuned models plus larger reasoning models (Qwen-3-32B, Llama-3.3-70B), and four complementary evaluation angles (Biasing Features, Filler Tokens, FUR, faithful@k, Logit Lens, CMA). This is a substantial amount of work and the replication of prior unfaithfulness results is a useful sanity check.

Transparency about limitations is above average for this venue: the paper openly reports the LLM-as-judge precision/recall (36%/31%), the cherry-picking concern with faithful@k, and the incompleteness-vs-non-exhaustiveness ambiguity. Reproducibility appears reasonable (code link, appendices with hyperparameters, control metrics for FUR, judge prompt shown in Fig. 29).
The paper is generally well written and clearly organized, with informative figures and clearly enumerated claims (T1, T2, T3.1, T3.2), which makes the argument easy to follow and to critique.
weaknesses: The Causal Mediation Analysis, which is central to the paper's headline claim that non-verbalized CoTs 'causally mediate' the hint's effect, rests on practically negligible effect sizes. NDE/NIE estimates are on the order of 1e-6 to 1e-11 in probability mass (Figs. 8, 9, 19-24). With 10,000 bootstrap resamples one can obtain 'confidence intervals excluding zero' for effects that are operationally zero. The claim that 'even non-verbilized hints can causally mediate prediction changes through the CoT' is therefore not credibly supported by this evidence, and the qualitative interpretation (suppression of alternatives, etc.) is built on differences among these vanishing quantities.

The faithful@k metric is fundamentally a best-of-k / pass@k construction: it asks whether at least one of k samples verbalizes the hint. This conflates 'the model can occasionally produce a verbalizing CoT' with 'the model is faithful,' and directly licenses cherry-picking. The paper's defense — that growth is concentrated under the Professor hint while Black Squares/Metadata stay flat — is itself consistent with a sycophancy explanation (which the paper explicitly acknowledges but does not rule out), so the divergence is at least as consistent with a confound as with the incompleteness hypothesis. The Limitations section concedes this cannot be resolved at the instance level.

The verbalization detector (gpt-oss-20b LLM-as-judge) has very low precision (36%) and recall (31%). Since the entire Biasing Features classification — and therefore the population of 'unfaithful' CoTs studied throughout — depends on this detector, this is a serious measurement problem. The authors had access to a stronger judge (gpt-4o, 80% precision) but deliberately used the weaker one to save cost; the mitigation (re-running on a lexically-non-verbilized subset) does not address false positives in the verbalization classification.

The logical gap at the core of the thesis is not closed. Showing that Filler Tokens/FUR classify many Biasing-Features-unfaithful CoTs as faithful demonstrates metric disagreement, not that the flagged CoTs are faithful (or 'incomplete') representations of the model's reasoning. The alternative metrics (Filler Tokens, FUR) are treated as a more valid ground truth without justification, yet they embody their own narrow definitions (prediction invariance under ellipsis; unlearning-based step importance) that are equally arguable. The paper's conclusion that 'unfaithfulness may reflect incompleteness rather than misalignment' is therefore stronger than what the evidence establishes.

Several claims are over-stated relative to the evidence (e.g., 'CoTs can causally mediate the hint's influence on model predictions' at 1e-6; 'much apparent unfaithfulness is due to tight token limits' when the budget analysis is confounded). The headline 'Can Be Faithful without Hint Verbalization' is not demonstrated; at best the paper shows that hint verbalization is one narrow proxy among several.

Conceptual novelty is limited: the observation that CoT explanations are incomplete and that hint-verbilization metrics are narrow has been raised in prior work (including sources the paper cites), and the contribution is primarily a re-evaluation and methodological caution rather than a new mechanism, metric, or theory. The proposed 'broader interpretability toolkit' is largely a recommendation to combine existing methods.
